subject: physics
title: Doppler effect for sound
key_idea: When a source of sound moves relative to a stationary observer, the observed frequency differs from the source frequency. Approaching gives a higher frequency, receding a lower one: fₒ = fₛ v / (v ± vₛ).

sections.heading: Why the pitch seems to change

blocks.text: A moving source of sound makes a stationary observer hear a different frequency from the one it emits. This is the Doppler effect.

items.text: The source emits waves at its source frequency fₛ.
Each wavefront is emitted closer to the observer than the last, so the wavefronts bunch up. The wavelength is shorter.
The speed of sound is fixed by the air, so a shorter wavelength means a higher observed frequency.
The wavefronts spread out behind the source. The wavelength is longer and the observed frequency is lower.

items: The effect depends on relative motion along the line between source and observer.
The source frequency does not change. Only the frequency the observer detects changes.
The effect for a moving observer and a stationary source is not needed.
A source moving towards a stationary observer gives a higher observed frequency.
A source moving away gives a lower observed frequency.

blocks.text: For a source moving along the line to a stationary observer, use this expression.

blocks.label: Observed frequency
where: v = speed of sound in air (m/s)

items: Use v − vₛ when the source moves towards the observer. The denominator is smaller, so fₒ is greater.
Use v + vₛ when the source moves away. The denominator is larger, so fₒ is smaller.

diagram.question: An ambulance siren has a frequency of {fs} Hz. It moves towards a stationary observer at {vs} m/s. Take the speed of sound as 340 m/s. Calculate the observed frequency.

items: fₒ = fₛ v / (v ± vₛ): minus when approaching, plus when receding.
The expression is for a source moving more slowly than sound.

checks.q: A source of frequency 600 Hz moves at 20 m/s towards a stationary observer. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Calculate the observed frequency.
The same source moves away at 20 m/s. Calculate the observed frequency.
Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why the observed frequency rises when a source approaches.
checks.a: Successive wavefronts are emitted from positions closer to the observer, so the wavelength reaching the observer is shorter. The wave speed is unchanged, so the frequency (v / λ) is higher.
